Japan's 2027 Subaru WRX STI Sport R Brings the TY85 Heavy-Duty Manual Transmission Back
16 photos
Photo: Subaru / edited
Subaru has finally given Japanese car enthusiasts a regular-production manual for the VB-series WRX, and the TY85 is no regular manual. Boasting a solid mechanical rod linkage instead of a cable-operated setup for the TY75, the new tranny is paired with a familiar 2.4-liter turbo four-pot boxer and Symmetrical permanent all-wheel drive.
The STI Sport R for Japan should not be confused for a revival of the STI, though. There is no additional horsepower or torque, and the newcomer does not feature the Driver Controlled Center Differential of the VA-series WRX STI. Instead, a viscous-coupling center differential will have to suffice. The Japanese-market WRX lost its regular manual option when the previous-gen STI ended production.
Subaru rolled out the VB-generation S4 in 2021, but offered it exclusively with the continuously variable Subaru Performance Transmission. Between you and me, this box is anything but sporty. Enthusiasts got a small reprieve with the STI Sport#, a limited-run WRX for Japan that required a lottery to secure.
The response to the STI Sport+ was hardly subtle, with Subaru reporting more than 9,000 applications versus the 600-unit production run. Considering that the WRX STI Sport R with the TY85 targets monthly sales of 330 units in the automaker's home market, it should cross the 600-unit mark no later than January 2027.
Photo: Subaru Subaru ended TY85 production back in 2019 alongside the VA-series WRX STI. Being a heavy-duty box, said transmission uses a reinforced case, gears, and bearings, along with cast-iron shift forks, sliding ball bearings, double-cone synchros for 1st, 2nd, and reverse, plus a triple-cone synchronizer for 2nd. The shifter mechanism reduces shift play by a claimed 60 percent.
Better in terms of torque capacity over the TY75 as well, the TY85 is a clear upgrade. No upgrades can be found directly under the hood, though, for the FA24 engine produces the very same 271 horsepower as the CVT-powered S4 version of the WRX for Japan. However, it does generate a bit more peak torque.
Subaru claims 375 Newton-meters (277 pound-feet) from 2,000 through 4,800 revolutions per minute, and the Japanese automaker has also improved boost pressure response for a more rewarding driving experience. Subaru 's objective is linear and immediate torque delivery, and Subaru has also catered to the less talented among us by integrating automatic rev-matching technology.
Photo: Subaru Despite returning to the TY85, the STI Sport R does not feature the DCCD system we all know and love from the WRX STI. Its viscous coupler is joined by an open front diff and an open rear differential. In other words, side-to-side torque transfer is handled electronically through brake actuation. A front helical diff and a rear Torsen unit would have been so much cooler, but hey, it is what it is.
ZF is listed as the supplier of the STI Sport R's electronically controlled dampers, which feature dedicated tuning for winding roads, while Brembo manufactures the front six-piston brake calipers and rear two-piston units, along with all four drilled rotors. The monoblocks in question are joined by a Sport+ drive mode that is said to sharpen torque response.
Touring Assist, Lane Departure Prevention, and Emergency Lane Keep Assist are some of the standard EyeSight driver-assist suite's highlights. At launch, eight paint colors are on the menu, including WR Blue Pearl. Japanese customers have to spend 5,480,000 yen at the very least to get their hands on the STI Sport R, a figure that converts to 34,300 dollars at current exchange rates.
